newsitem.title: MEXICO: Mexico ruling party far behind in key race - poll.
newsitem.headline: Mexico ruling party far behind in key race - poll.

text.p: President Ernesto Zedillo's party was trailing a poor third behind both main opposition parties in the first-ever mayoral election race in Mexico's capital, according to a poll made available to Reuters on Friday ahead of publication.
The Indemerc/Louis Harris poll, the latest in a series of tracking surveys for July's key Mexico City race, showed Zedillo's Institutional Revolutionary Party (PRI) has a dismal 14 percent of voters.

The Mexico City mayoral race, part of wider July elections that include congressional and gubernatorial contests, was considered hugely important because of the city's great size and its disproportionate political and economic weight.

Until now, the mayor was chosen directly by the president and has always been a PRI man. The PRI has typically won elections with a 40 to 50 percent share of the vote, but was more unpopular in Mexico City than in the rest of the country.

The conservative National Action Party (PAN) leads voter preferences but its support fell to 36 percent in January from 40 percent in December, according to Indemerc, which has a good track record of predicting Mexican elections.
But the PAN has a problem with its candidate. The man who was by far its most popular potential nominee, Diego Fernandez de Cevallos, has repeatedly insisted he does not want to run.
No other party figure commands anything near Fernandez de Cevallos's 35 to 40 percent levels of support.

The two PAN runners for the nomination announced so far, former party President Carlos Castillo Peraza and Mexico City politician Francisco Jose Paoli, have ratings of just 20 percent and 15 percent respectively.

The big surprise of January's Indemerc survey was the growing voter enthusiasm for the left-wing Party of the Democratic Revolution (PRD), which favours an end to privatisation and more socialist economic policies.
Indemerc/Louis Harris said 24 percent of those polled backed the PRD, the highest level of support the party has won in the capital since it began tracking in November 1995.

Further boosting the PRD's hopes, the poll showed that its former presidential candidate Cuauhtemoc Cardenas was the second most popular potential candidate among voters, with a 30 percent rating in January.
The parties have yet to choose their official candidates.
The survey of 600 adults was conducted on Jan. 25-28 in Mexico City and has a margin of error of 3.5 percentage points.
